Create the account on your phone

A Gmail account is part of a **Google Account**. The same account opens Gmail, Google Drive, Google Meet, Google Docs and the Play Store, so you only need one password for all of them. It is free. Make sure you have some data or Wi-Fi and about ten minutes.

Type your first name and surname, then your date of birth and gender. Google uses the birth date to apply age rules, so enter it truthfully.
Pick your Gmail address from the suggestions, or tap **Create your own Gmail address** and type the one you planned.
Create a strong password: at least 8 characters, best as a short phrase with numbers and symbols, for example a sentence only you would know. Write it somewhere safe at home, not in your phone notes.
Add your phone number when asked. Google sends a code by SMS to confirm it is you, and the number helps you get back in if you forget your password.
Read the privacy terms, tap **I agree**, and your inbox opens.

Tone, Formality and Writing for Your Reader
Match greetings and closings to formal, semi-formal and friendly situations
Rewrite a blunt or overly casual message into a polite, clear one
Avoid tone mistakes such as all capital letters, slang and too many exclamation marks
Write a short email to a senior person that is respectful without being stiff

In a face-to-face conversation your voice, smile and body language soften your words. In an email the reader only has the words. A short message that you meant as quick can feel rude, and a long, flowery one can feel confusing. **Tone** is the feeling your words create. Good tone comes from thinking about who will read the email and what relationship you have with them.
Three levels of formality
Level
When to use it
Closing
Formal
First contact, senior officials, job applications, banks, complaints
Dear Mrs Okafor, / Dear Sir or Madam,

Semi-formal

When you are not sure, choose one step more formal than you think. It is easy to relax once the other person writes casually, but it is hard to repair a first impression of being too familiar. In Nigeria, titles matter: if someone signs as Dr, Engr, Barr or Pastor, use that title in your reply until they invite you to use their first name.

Friendly: close colleagues
Semi-formal: known contacts

The wider the base, the more often you need it: most first emails at work should start formal.
Words that change the feeling

Small words do a lot of work. **Please** and **thank you** cost nothing. Phrases such as **could you**, **would it be possible** and **I would appreciate** turn an order into a request. Avoid writing whole sentences in CAPITAL LETTERS, because readers feel shouted at. Use one exclamation mark at most, and avoid text-speak like pls, u, tnx and abeg in formal email. Emojis are fine with friends but not in a first message to a manager or official.

Before you send, read your email as if you were the person receiving it.
Worked example: from blunt to professional
For example, Funmi coordinates volunteers for a community health outreach in Ibadan. She needs the venue manager, whom she has never met, to confirm the hall for Saturday 14th.
Her first draft reads: Hello, we need the hall on Saturday. Confirm today. Funmi.
She checks the reader: a stranger and a manager, so she moves to formal tone.
She adds a clear subject: Request to confirm hall booking for Saturday 14th.

She rewrites the body: Dear Mr Adeyemi, I am writing on behalf of the WODDI health outreach team. We would like to confirm the booking of the main hall for Saturday 14th from 9 am to 2 pm for about 60 people. Could you kindly confirm availability by Thursday, so that we can inform our volunteers? Thank you for your help.
She closes with: Kind regards, Funmi Ade, Volunteer Coordinator, phone 080X XXX XXXX.
The new email is 72 words instead of 12, but it answers every question the manager would have: who, what, when, how many and by when. He replies the same day with a confirmation.
Read it aloud before you send
Read the email aloud quietly. If a sentence sounds harsh when spoken, soften it.
Check the name and title of the person are spelled correctly.
Remove anything you would not want forwarded to someone else, because emails are easily forwarded.
If you are angry, save it as a draft and read it again after an hour.
Culture and respect

Many readers in Nigeria and across Africa expect a short courtesy before business, such as I hope you are well. One line is enough. Then go straight to the point, because busy people appreciate brevity.
Replying to someone senior

When your manager, a pastor or a government officer writes to you, mirror their level. If they wrote Dear Mrs Bello and signed with their full title, reply in the same formal way. If they wrote Hi Kemi, thanks, you may relax a little, but keep full sentences and correct spelling. Answer every question they asked, in the same order they asked them. If you cannot give a full answer yet, say when you will: Thank you, sir. I will send the figures by Wednesday afternoon. A short, respectful reply sent quickly is better than a perfect reply sent a week later.

When unsure, write one level more formal.

Subject Lines, Clear Requests and Attachments That Get Replies
Write specific subject lines that show the topic and any action or deadline
Structure an email so the main request appears in the first two lines
Attach files correctly, name them clearly and share large files as Drive links
Follow up politely when you get no reply

Busy people decide in a few seconds whether to open, postpone or ignore an email. Two things drive that decision: the **subject line** and the first two lines of the body, which the inbox shows as a preview. If these are clear, you are far more likely to get a reply.
Subject lines that work

A good subject line is specific and short, usually 4 to 9 words. It names the topic and, where needed, the action and the date. Never leave the subject empty: many people skip emails with no subject, and some spam filters treat them as suspicious.
Weak subject
Strong subject
Hello
Application for Sales Assistant role: Ngozi Eze
Urgent!!!
Please approve venue payment by Friday 5 pm
Documents
Signed membership forms for Lagos group (3 PDFs)
Meeting
Agenda for Tuesday 10 am finance meeting
(no subject)
Question about my certificate name spelling
Put the request first

Use the **BLUF** method, which stands for Bottom Line Up Front. State what you need in the first sentence or two, then give the background. Many writers do the opposite: they explain for three paragraphs and hide the question at the end, where it is missed.
A reply-friendly email structure
Specific subject line
Request in first two lines
Short supporting details
Clear deadline
Polite close and signature
Readers act fastest when the request comes first and the details follow.
Ask one main question per email, or number your questions 1, 2, 3 so each gets an answer.
Give a real deadline with day and time, for example by Thursday 12 noon, rather than ASAP.
Keep paragraphs to 2 to 4 lines. Long blocks of text are hard to read on a phone.
End with what happens next, for example Once you confirm, I will send the invoice.
A paper clip icon representing an email attachment
The paper clip is where you add files; always check the file is really attached before sending.
Attachments done properly
Rename the file before you attach it so the reader knows what it is: Ngozi_Eze_CV_2026.pdf, not IMG_20260412_093311.jpg or Document1.
Send documents as **PDF** where possible, because a PDF looks the same on every phone and computer. Most phones can save a document as PDF using Print then Save as PDF.
Mention the attachment in the body: I have attached my CV and a scanned copy of my certificate.
Keep total attachments under 25 MB. If Gmail finds the file is bigger, it offers to send it as a Google Drive link instead; accept that, and make sure the link is shared with the reader.
Before sending, look for the file name under your message. Gmail may warn you if you wrote attached but forgot the file, but do not rely on it.
Worked example: a job application email
For example, Amina in Kaduna saw a vacancy for a Front Desk Officer at a clinic. The advert says to email a CV and cover letter to the HR address by 30th.
Subject: Application for Front Desk Officer: Amina Bello.
Opening lines: Dear Hiring Manager, I am applying for the Front Desk Officer position advertised on your noticeboard. I have attached my CV and cover letter as PDFs.
Details, one short paragraph: I have three years of reception experience at a pharmacy, I am comfortable with Microsoft Word and Excel, and I live 10 minutes from the clinic.
Close: I am available for an interview any weekday. Thank you for considering my application. Yours sincerely, Amina Bello, 080X XXX XXXX.
Attachments: Amina_Bello_CV.pdf (310 KB) and Amina_Bello_Cover_Letter.pdf (120 KB). Total 430 KB, far below the 25 MB limit.
The HR officer can see the role, the applicant and the attachments without opening anything else. Amina also gets a copy in her Sent folder as proof she applied before the deadline.
Following up without nagging

If you get no reply, wait a reasonable time: about 3 working days for normal requests, or until one day before a deadline for urgent ones. Reply to your own original email so the history stays in one thread, and keep it short: Dear Mr Musa, I am following up on my email below about the hall booking. Could you let me know by Thursday? Thank you.
Undo Send and Schedule send

In Gmail settings you can set Undo Send to give you up to 30 seconds to stop an email after tapping Send. You can also tap the three dots beside Send and choose Schedule send, so a message written at midnight arrives at 8 am.

Finally, add an **email signature** so every message ends with your details automatically. In the Gmail app open Settings, choose your account and tap Mobile signature. Keep it to three or four lines: your full name, your role or business, and a phone number. Leave out quotes, long slogans and large images, which make emails heavy on data.

An inbox with 3,000 unread emails hides the one message that matters, such as an interview invitation or a payment confirmation. Gmail gives you tools to stay on top of it. Most of them take a few seconds once you know where they are.
Labels instead of folders

Many email programs use **folders**. Gmail uses **labels**, which work like folders but are more flexible: one email can carry two labels, for example Customers and Invoices. To create one in the app, open an email, tap the three dots, choose **Change labels**, then create a new label. Labels appear in the side menu so you can open all emails with that label at once.

Filters: sorting mail automatically

A **filter** applies a rule to new email, for example: anything from the bank gets the Bank label and skips the inbox. Filters are created on a computer or in a phone browser set to the desktop site, not inside the Gmail app. In the search bar, tap the options icon, enter the sender or words, then click **Create filter** and choose the action, such as Apply the label or Skip the Inbox.
Worked example: cleaning up a crowded inbox
For example, Chioma, who sells fabrics in Onitsha, has 1,240 unread emails, mostly shop newsletters, and has missed two customer orders.
She searches is:unread category:promotions and finds about 900 adverts. She selects them and archives them in one go on the computer.
She opens three newsletters she never reads and taps Unsubscribe at the top of each.
She creates two labels, Orders and Suppliers, and labels the 25 order emails she finds by searching order.
She creates a filter: emails containing the word order get the Orders label and a star.
She stars the two missed customer orders and replies to both that afternoon with an apology.
Her inbox drops from 1,240 to about 60 unread emails in under an hour, and new orders now arrive starred so she cannot miss them.
Spam: what to do

**Spam** is unwanted bulk email, often adverts, and sometimes scams. Gmail moves much of it to the Spam folder automatically and deletes it after 30 days. If spam reaches your inbox, open it, tap the three dots and choose **Report spam**. This trains the filter. If a real email lands in Spam, open it and tap **Report not spam** so future emails from that sender arrive normally.
Do not click links in suspicious emails

Emails that promise prizes, threaten that your account will be closed, or ask you to confirm your BVN or bank details are usually phishing scams. Do not click links or open attachments in them. Report them as spam and delete them. Module 4 covers phishing in detail.

Worked example: a uniform proposal to a school
For example, Patience is a tailor in Benin City. The head teacher of a private primary school mentioned that 40 pupils need new uniforms before resumption in September.
The need: 40 pupils need new uniforms (shirt and shorts or skirt) in school colours before resumption on 8th September.
Your solution: sew 40 sets in sizes from the class list, using fabric matched to the school's sample, with two fittings at the school.
Cost table: 40 sets at ₦9,500 each (approximate market rate in her area) equals ₦380,000. Delivery to the school included. Price valid for 14 days.
Timeline: measurements 4th August, first fitting 18th August, delivery 1st September. Payment: 50 percent (₦190,000) deposit, balance on delivery.
Why you: five years sewing school and church uniforms, photos of past work attached, references from two schools available.
Next step: Please confirm by 25th July so that I can buy fabric in time.

Summary in two lines: The total is ₦380,000 with delivery on 1st September. A 50 percent deposit confirms the order.
Next step: I would be grateful for your decision by 25th July. I am happy to bring fabric samples to the school.
Close: Kind regards, Patience Okun, Patience Stitches, 080X XXX XXXX.

**Numbers:** how many people attended, how much was spent, items distributed. Use a table.
**Challenges:** what went wrong, honestly, and how it was handled.
**Lessons and next steps:** what you would do differently and what comes next.

Read the previous messages before asking a question that may already be answered. Reply to a specific message by swiping on it so others know what you are answering. Copying people has meaning. Cc a manager when they need to know about a decision, not to put pressure on a colleague. If you copy someone's boss on a complaint before speaking to the person directly, it can feel like an attack. When you add someone new to a long thread, write a line at the top for them: Adding Mrs Bello, who handles payments. Mrs Bello, please see the invoice question below. When someone is no longer needed on a thread, it is polite to move them to Bcc with a note: Moving Kemi to Bcc to spare her inbox. The rest of the thread then continues without her.

Sooner or later you will receive an angry customer message, a harsh email from a colleague, or a complaint you have to make yourself. Online, misunderstandings grow quickly because there is no tone of voice. The aim is always the same: protect the relationship, solve the problem, and keep a fair written record.
First, pause

Your first reply should never be written in anger. Read the message twice. Separate the facts (the order was two days late) from the feelings (I am very disappointed). If you feel your heart racing, wait at least an hour or until the next morning. You can send a short holding reply: Thank you for letting me know. I am looking into this and will reply fully by 3 pm.
The LAST method for replies

Acknowledge the feeling
Solve: offer a fix
Thank them
Following these four steps keeps your reply calm and focused on solving the problem.
Step
Example phrase

Acknowledge

Solve

Worked example: replying to an angry customer

For example, Joy runs a cake business in Lagos. A customer, Tunde, sends this WhatsApp message at 4 pm: This is unacceptable!!! The cake came 3 hours late and my guests had already left. I want my money back.
Joy pauses, then checks the facts: the dispatch rider left late because of traffic and she did not warn Tunde.
Listen and acknowledge: Good afternoon Tunde. I am truly sorry the cake arrived at 3 pm instead of 12 noon, and that it affected your celebration.
Take responsibility without excuses: I should have called you as soon as I knew the rider was delayed.
Solve: I would like to refund the ₦5,000 delivery fee and 30 percent of the cake price, ₦9,000, a total of ₦14,000, today. Is that acceptable to you?
Thank and follow through: Thank you for telling me directly. She sends the transfer, shares the receipt, and adds a rule for herself to call customers if delivery will be more than 30 minutes late.
Tunde accepts the ₦14,000 refund and replies that he appreciates the honesty. The full exchange is in writing, which protects both sides.
Writing your own complaint
Send it to the right place: the company's official email or customer service channel, not a public post first.
Use a clear subject: Complaint: order 4521 delivered damaged on 3 June.
State the facts in order: what you bought, when, the reference number, what went wrong.
Attach evidence: receipt, photos, screenshots of earlier messages.
Say exactly what you want: a replacement, a refund of a stated amount, or a repair, and by when.
Stay polite. Firm and factual gets results faster than angry.
When to stop typing

If a conversation has gone back and forth more than three times without progress, or emotions are high, suggest a call: I think it will be quicker to talk. Are you free for a 10-minute call at 5 pm? After the call, send a short message confirming what you agreed. That way you get the warmth of speaking and still keep a record.
Never in public, never in anger

Do not argue in public comments or groups, and do not post screenshots of private conversations to shame someone. It damages your reputation more than theirs, and it may break privacy rules. Handle disagreements privately, and if someone threatens or harasses you, stop replying, keep the evidence and report or block them.
When you made the mistake

Everyone sends a wrong figure, forgets an attachment or emails the wrong person at some point. Correct it quickly and simply. Reply in the same thread with a subject that starts Correction:, state the right information, and apologise once without drama: Correction: the meeting is on Thursday 12th, not Tuesday. Sorry for the confusion. If you sent private information to the wrong person, ask them politely to delete it, and tell the person whose information it was. Owning a mistake in one or two lines builds more trust than a long excuse.

Talk about the work, not the person: The budget is ₦20,000 over the limit, not You always overspend.
Ask questions before concluding: Can you help me understand how we got this figure?
Offer a way forward: Could we reduce printing to 100 copies to bring it within budget?

Online Safety: Phishing, Scams, Passwords and 2-Step Verification
Spot the warning signs of phishing emails, SMS and WhatsApp messages
Check a sender's address and a link before clicking

Know what to do immediately if you clicked a scam link or shared details

**Phishing** is when criminals pretend to be a trusted organisation, such as your bank, Google, a delivery company or even WODDI, to trick you into giving passwords, PINs, codes or money. It arrives by email, SMS, WhatsApp, phone call and social media. Phishing works because it creates panic or excitement, so you act before you think. The best protection is to slow down and check.
Warning signs
Phishing red flags
Urgent threat or prize
Sender address looks wrong
Link goes somewhere strange
Asks for PIN, password, code
Generic greeting, poor spelling
If a message shows even one of these signs, stop and verify before you act.
**Urgency or threats:** Your account will be blocked in 24 hours. Your BVN must be updated today.
**Too good to be true:** You have won ₦500,000. A grant for women is available, pay ₦5,000 processing fee.
**Wrong sender address:** the name says GTBank or Google, but the address is gtbank-security@gmail.com or something like goog1e-support.com.
**Strange links:** on a phone, press and hold a link to preview the real web address without opening it. If it does not match the real organisation's website, do not tap it.
**Requests for secrets:** no genuine bank, telecom company or Google will ask for your PIN, password, OTP or full card number by message or call.
**Unexpected attachments:** files you did not expect, especially ones that ask you to enable something to view them.
A phone showing a secure login screen with a lock
Strong passwords and 2-Step Verification keep criminals out even if they learn part of your login.
Worked example: checking a suspicious bank email
For example, Ifeoma receives an email: Dear Customer, unusual activity detected on your account. Click here within 2 hours to verify your details or your account will be suspended.
She notices the generic greeting Dear Customer and the 2-hour threat: two red flags.
She taps the sender name to see the full address: alerts@secure-bankverify.net, not her bank's official domain.
She presses and holds the link: it points to a strange web address unrelated to her bank.
She does not click. In Gmail she taps the three dots and chooses Report spam (on a computer she can choose Report phishing), then deletes it.
To be sure, she opens her bank app directly, not from the email, and sees no alerts. She also calls the number printed on the back of her ATM card.
Her account is fine. By checking the sender, previewing the link and contacting the bank through an official channel, she avoided giving her login to criminals.
Strong passwords
Use a different password for your email than for any other account. Your email can reset all your other passwords, so it must be the strongest.
Make it long: a passphrase of three or four unrelated words with a number and symbol, such as a sentence about something only you know, is stronger and easier to remember than a short jumble.
Never use your name, birthday, phone number or 123456.
Consider a password manager, such as Google Password Manager built into Chrome and Android, so you do not have to remember every password.
Switch on 2-Step Verification

**2-Step Verification** (2SV) means that signing in needs your password plus a second proof, such as a prompt on your phone or a code. Even if a criminal learns your password, they cannot get in without your phone.
Open the Gmail app, tap your profile picture, then **Manage your Google Account**.
Tap the **Security** tab (you may need to scroll the tabs sideways).
Under How you sign in to Google, tap **2-Step Verification** and follow the steps to turn it on.
Choose Google prompts or SMS codes, and also save the **backup codes** on paper at home in case you lose your phone.
Do the same for WhatsApp: Settings, Account, Two-step verification, and create a 6-digit PIN.
If you clicked or shared details

Act immediately. If you gave bank details, call your bank's official number at once and ask them to block the card or account. Change your email password from a safe device and sign out of all other sessions in your Google Account security page. Turn on 2-Step Verification. Warn your contacts if your WhatsApp or email may have been used to send scam messages. Keep screenshots as evidence.

Finally, protect other people too. Do not forward suspicious messages, even to warn friends, because others may click the link. Describe the scam in your own words instead, and report fake accounts to the platform. Be extra careful on public Wi-Fi in hotels or eateries: avoid logging into bank apps there, and use your own mobile data for anything involving money.

Professional email: set up, write well, and stay organised.

Why it matters
Email is your written record
Banks, schools and employers use email
It can be searched, forwarded and kept
One free Google Account opens Gmail and more
A good address and a clear email win replies
Banks, schools, employers and government offices still send formal messages by email.
A WhatsApp chat is quick, but an email is a written record that can be searched, forwarded and kept for years.
Let us see how to choose a good address, write emails that get replies, and keep your inbox tidy.
Your address
Choose a professional address
ngozicakes.enugu@gmail.com
Your address is the first thing a stranger sees. A nickname may be fun among friends, but an employer may not take it seriously.
Use your real name in a simple pattern. If it is taken, add a middle initial, your trade or your town, not random numbers.
The email screen
Know every box before you send
To: the people who must act
Cc: people kept informed; everyone sees them
Bcc: hidden addresses, to protect privacy
Subject: what the email is about
Attachment: up to 25 MB, or send a Drive link
Tap Compose. The To box is for the people who must read and act.
Cc, carbon copy, keeps people informed. Everyone can see who was copied.
Bcc, blind carbon copy, hides addresses. Use it to protect privacy when you email a group.
The subject tells the reader what the email is about before they open it.
The paper clip adds files, up to 25 MB. Bigger files go as a Google Drive link.
Step by step
Write an email that gets a reply
Specific subject: topic, action, date
Greeting that fits the reader
Request in the first two lines
Short details and a real deadline
Polite close, your name, then read aloud
Step one. A specific subject of 4 to 9 words, like Please approve venue payment by Friday 5 pm. Never leave it empty.
Step two. Fit the greeting to the reader. Dear Mrs Okafor for a senior person or stranger, Hello Mr Musa for someone you know.
Step three. Put your request in the first two lines. This is called Bottom Line Up Front, so the question is not hidden at the end.
Step four. Short details, and a real deadline with day and time, not ASAP.
Step five. Close politely and read it aloud. Please and could you turn an order into a request. No capital-letter shouting, no text-speak like pls.
When unsure, choose one step more formal. It is easy to relax later, but hard to repair a first impression.
Worked example
Amina applies for a job by email
Mention the attachment in the body, then check it is there.
Subject: Application for Front Desk Officer
First lines: the role, and CV attached
One short paragraph of experience
Close: available for interview, full name
Files renamed clearly, sent as PDF
For example, Amina in Kaduna applies to be a Front Desk Officer at a clinic. Her subject names the role and her name.
Her first lines say which job, and that her CV and cover letter are attached as PDFs.
One short paragraph: three years of reception experience, and she lives 10 minutes away.
She closes with Yours sincerely, her full name and phone number.
Her files are renamed clearly, not IMG and a long number. Together they are 430 KB, far below 25 MB.
Her Sent folder keeps proof she applied before the deadline.

Label, star and archive; report spam

Greeting message for new customers
Away message outside working hours

Worked example
Ada handles a night-time order
Confirm decisions in writing, and check payment in your bank app.
9:40 pm: away message replies for her
8:05 am: label New order, send /price

For example, Ada runs a catering business in Abuja. On Friday at 9:40 pm, Kunle asks the price of small chops for 30 people. Her away message replies that she will answer from 8 am.
At 8:05 am she labels the chat New order and types slash price to send her saved list.
She greets him by name and quotes the medium package, approximately 45,000 naira, and asks when and where the event is.
When he replies, she confirms everything in one message: Saturday 20th, delivery to Garki by 11 am, 45,000 naira, 50 percent deposit to confirm.
After payment she changes the label to Paid and emails a simple invoice as a record.
Two habits protect you here. Confirm agreements in writing. And confirm payment in your bank app before delivering, because fake payment screenshots are a common trick.

Unmute, speak, then mute again. Say your name the first time you speak.
Ask questions in the chat, or raise your hand in a large meeting and wait to be called.

Reply once, calmly
Explain your quality and offer
Invite them to message you

Why it matters
Writing that people act on
A short proposal that is easy to say yes to
Minutes that settle arguments later
Group messages people do not mute
Calm replies when things go wrong
A proposal is a written offer: I can solve this problem, in this way, for this cost, by this date.
Groups forget. Written minutes settle what was decided, who promised what, and how much was spent.
Writing to a whole group brings new problems, like exposed addresses and noisy chats.
And online, misunderstandings grow quickly, because there is no tone of voice.
Step by step
Only promise dates you can meet.
The need: what problem, for whom
Your solution: what you will do or supply
Cost and timeline: a small table
Why you: evidence in 2 to 3 sentences
Next step: one sentence with a date
Step one, the need. In 2 to 3 sentences, say what problem you are solving and for whom.
Step two, your solution. A short list of exactly what you will do or supply.
Step three, cost and timeline. Break the cost down, say what is included, and how long the price is valid, for example 14 days.
Step four, why you. Give evidence, such as photos of past work or references.
Step five, the next step. Tell the reader what to do now, and by when.
Save it as a PDF, so the layout cannot move.
A realistic date kept is better than an early date missed.
Worked example
Patience quotes for school uniforms
For example, Patience, a tailor in Benin City, quotes for 40 school uniforms.
40 sets at this price each
50 percent deposit
Delivery included. Naira prices are approximate.
Here is a worked example. Patience is a tailor in Benin City. A head teacher needs uniforms for 40 pupils before resumption.
She prices each set at 9,500 naira, an approximate market rate in her area.
Her payment terms are clear: a 50 percent deposit of 190,000 naira, and the balance on delivery.
40 sets at 9,500 naira is 380,000 naira in total, with delivery included, valid for 14 days.
The head teacher checks the sums easily, and approves it at the next board meeting.
What good minutes record
Group, date, time and place or platform
Who was present and who sent apologies
Decisions, exactly, with figures
Action points: task, person, deadline
Next meeting date
Minutes are a short record, not every word. Start with the group name, date, time and place, or the platform, such as Google Meet.
List who was present and who sent apologies.
Write decisions exactly, with figures. For example, Hauwa's savings group recorded that the May payout of 240,000 naira goes to Fatima.
Each action point needs a task, a person and a deadline.
Then the next meeting date. Type the minutes the same day and share them within 2 days, while memories are fresh.
Groups
Writing to many people
Do
Reply by default
Yourself in To, members in Bcc
Announcement-only WhatsApp group
Ask before adding anyone
Reply all with Thank you
Everyone's address on show
Chain messages and rumours
Posting personal information
Use Reply by default. For an announcement, put your own address in To and all members in Bcc, so addresses stay private and nobody can Reply all.
In WhatsApp, an admin can make an announcement group where only admins post, with a separate group for discussion.
Avoid Reply all for a simple thank you. Sent to 80 people, it wastes 80 people's time.
Check facts before forwarding. A message labelled Forwarded many times is more likely to be false.
Difficult messages
The LAST method for complaints
Never reply in anger. Pause first.
Listen: show you understood the problem
Acknowledge the feeling, without arguing
Solve: offer a specific fix
First, pause. Read the message twice and separate the facts from the feelings. If you are upset, wait at least an hour.
Then use LAST. Listen: show you have understood the actual problem.
Acknowledge: recognise the feeling without arguing. I am sorry, I know this affected your event.
Solve: offer a specific fix or a choice.
Thank: thank them for telling you. It helps you improve.
Joy makes it right
For example, Joy's cake for Tunde in Lagos arrived 3 hours late.
Delivery fee refunded
30 percent of the cake price
Refund paid the same day, with the receipt shared.
For example, Joy runs a cake business in Lagos. Tunde's cake arrived 3 hours late, and he is angry. Joy pauses and checks the facts. The rider was delayed, and she did not warn him.
She apologises, takes responsibility without excuses, and offers to refund the 5,000 naira delivery fee and 30 percent of the cake price, which is 9,000 naira.
That is 14,000 naira, paid today. Tunde accepts and thanks her for her honesty.
Joy adds a rule for herself: call the customer if delivery will be more than 30 minutes late.
Key points
Remember
Proposal: need, solution, cost, why you, next step
Minutes: decisions and action points
Members in Bcc; Reply all only when needed
Pause, then Listen, Acknowledge, Solve, Thank
Never argue in public or shame anyone
To remember. A proposal answers five questions. Minutes record decisions and action points. Protect members' addresses with Bcc. Pause, then use LAST.
And handle disagreements privately. After three unproductive exchanges, suggest a call, then confirm in writing.

Employers, customers and partners often search for you before they call.

Step by step
Audit and tidy what people find
Same name, same photo, same description everywhere.
Open a private or incognito tab
Search your full name in quotation marks
Check Images and your public profiles
Note anything outdated or embarrassing
Delete, untag or update it
Step one. Open a private or incognito tab, so your own accounts do not affect results.
Step two. Search Google for your full name in quotation marks, then with your town, and with your trade.
Step three. Check the Images tab, and look at your own profiles as the public sees them.
Step four. Write down anything outdated, embarrassing or inconsistent.
Step five. Delete careless old posts, untag unwanted photos, and close pages you no longer use.

Your bio
One bio, three lengths
About 15 words, for Instagram and WhatsApp. What you do, where, and how to book.
About 40 words, for group introductions and your LinkedIn headline area.
About 90 words, for proposals and event programmes, with training and contact details.
For example, Halima is a bridal henna and makeup artist in Kaduna. Her one-line bio, about 15 words, says what she does, where, and that bookings are by WhatsApp.
Her short bio, about 40 words, is for group introductions and LinkedIn.
Her long bio, about 90 words, adds her training history and contact details for proposals.
She saves all three in a phone note called My bio, so when someone says, tell us about yourself, she replies in seconds.
The LinkedIn sections that matter
Professional photo, real name, location
Headline: what you do and for whom
About: three short paragraphs
Experience: action verbs and numbers
Personal note on every connection request
LinkedIn is a social network for work, like an online CV that is always available. Start with a good photo, your real name and location.
Your headline should say what you do and for whom, not only a job title.
Your About section: what you do, your experience and results, and what you are looking for.
Then experience. Use action verbs and numbers, like Managed weekly contributions for 25 members. Numbers make claims believable.
When you connect with someone new, add a note of one or two lines saying how you know of them.
Count all your work
Mercy's informal work, made visible
Before
Market trader, eight years
Association treasurer
Empty LinkedIn page
After
Owner, Mercy's Provisions
Treasurer: 40 members in Sheets
Found by NGO recruiters

Many women undervalue what they do. For example, Mercy has sold foodstuff at a market in Ibadan for eight years, and has been treasurer of her women's association for three. Her LinkedIn page was empty.
Now her first entry reads Owner, Mercy's Provisions, with about 150 regular customers. Her second reads Treasurer, recording contributions for 40 members in Google Sheets.
An NGO recruiter searching for record-keeping in Ibadan can now find her.
Stop and check if you see these
Urgent threat or a prize
Asks for PIN, password or code
Phishing is when criminals pretend to be your bank, Google or even WODDI, to trick you into giving passwords, codes or money.
If you see even one of these red flags, stop. Press and hold a link to preview the real address without opening it.
Worked example
Ifeoma checks a suspicious bank email
Contact your bank only through its app or official number.
Spots Dear Customer and a 2-hour threat
Checks the full sender address
Presses and holds the link to preview
Reports spam and deletes it
Opens her bank app directly
For example, Ifeoma gets an email: unusual activity on your account, click within 2 hours or your account will be suspended. Dear Customer and a threat. Two red flags.
She taps the sender name. The address is not her bank's official one.
She presses and holds the link. It points somewhere unrelated to her bank.
She does not click. She reports it as spam and deletes it.
To be sure, she opens her bank app directly, not from the email, and calls the number on the back of her ATM card. Her account is fine.
Protect yourself
Lock your accounts and act fast
A long passphrase, different for your email. Never your name, birthday or 123456.
Turn it on in your Google Account Security tab. Save backup codes on paper at home.
Call your bank's official number at once. Change your email password and sign out other sessions.
Your email can reset all your other passwords, so it needs the strongest one: a long passphrase that you use nowhere else.
Switch on 2-Step Verification in the Security tab of your Google Account. Then a criminal cannot get in without your phone, even with your password. Set a WhatsApp PIN too.
If you clicked or shared details, act immediately. Call your bank's official number to block the card or account. Change your email password from a safe device, and warn your contacts.
And remember, real employers never ask you to pay to get a job.

No genuine body asks for your PIN or OTP

To remember. Search yourself privately. Stay consistent everywhere. Count all your work, with numbers. Never give your PIN, password or OTP. And turn on 2-Step Verification today.
